Listen to this article Share When Donald Trump accused South Africa of perpetrating genocide against its white population, he raised a question extending far beyond that country: who gets to define genocide, and whose suffering commands the attention of powerful governments? The cases of South Africa, Gaza and Biafra suggest that law and evidence decide what genocide is, while power decides which claims are acted upon. Advertisement Advertisement White South Africans have suffered brutal crimes, including farm murders. Their suffering deserves recognition and justice. But violent crime affects South Africans across racial lines, disproportionately harming Black communities. Police figures recorded 19,696 murders between April and December 2024, of which 36 were farm-related, and 29 of those victims were farm workers, who are overwhelmingly Black. A South African court ruled in February 2025 that claims of a white genocide were “clearly imagined.” Available evidence does not establish a campaign to destroy white South Africans as a racial group. Genocide has a precise meaning under the 1948 Genocide Convention: prohibited acts committed with the intention of destroying, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Recognising suffering does not require accepting every political interpretation of it. Murder, persecution and genocide are serious crimes, but they are not interchangeable. Nigerians have had this argument before. Many Igbo people have long described the massacres of 1966 and the starvation and mass deaths of the Nigerian Civil War as genocide. Estimates of Igbo killed in 1966 run from about 10,000 to 30,000, and estimates of war deaths from 500,000 to 3 million, mostly civilians who starved. The classification remains contested, but the suffering is beyond dispute. Even then, the obligation to investigate atrocities, acknowledge suffering and protect civilians remains, and arguments over what to call a tragedy must never excuse denying that it occurred. Anyone may allege genocide. Establishing it requires evidence and legal scrutiny. Yet governments can act before courts rule, giving allegations political authority whether or not they are substantiated. Power turns allegations into policy. Trump’s claims helped justify preferential refugee arrangements for Afrikaners. In October 2025 his administration capped refugee admissions at 7,500, the lowest in the programme’s history and down from 125,000 the year before, and said the places would go primarily to Afrikaners. An allegation unsupported by credible evidence of genocide acquired the authority of American policy. Why should one minority receive exceptional protection when millions elsewhere flee persecution and displacement? Advertisement There is historical irony here. Under apartheid, South Africa’s white minority enjoyed privileges denied to the Black majority. That history does not invalidate present-day grievances, and no society committed to equality should make inherited guilt the price of protection. But context matters when claims of racial victimhood become instruments of international policy. Then there is Gaza. South Africa, the country Trump accuses of permitting genocide, brought a case before the International Court of Justice in December 2023 alleging that Israel violated the Genocide Convention. The situations are not legally or evidentially equivalent. The court has issued three binding provisional measures orders but has not ruled on whether genocide occurred, and after Israel’s March 2026 counter-memorial, which objected to the court’s jurisdiction, the written pleadings run to 2029. Separately, a UN Commission of Inquiry, which does not speak for the UN as a whole, concluded in September 2025, and reaffirmed in October 2026, that Israeli authorities and forces committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel rejects the allegation, maintaining that its campaign targets Hamas. The attacks of 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed, do not remove the obligation to examine Israel’s subsequent conduct under international law. South Africa has pursued its allegation through an international judicial process, yet investigators’ findings have not produced comparable willingness from Washington to confront a longstanding ally. Advertisement Colonialism established hierarchies of credibility alongside hierarchies of power. The coloniser’s account was presumed authoritative, while the colonised had to prove their injustices. Colonial violence was called maintaining order, and resistance savagery or rebellion. Under apartheid, powerful Western governments resisted comprehensive sanctions for years, and the US Congress imposed them in 1986 over President Reagan’s veto. Advertisement Advertisement These hierarchies also shape how nations remember their histories. Biafra shows that recognition stays contested long after violence ends. Nigeria’s struggle to confront Civil War suffering raises questions about whose memories enter the national narrative and whether reconciliation is possible without an honest reckoning. Alliances, ethnicity, domestic politics and economic interests shape responses too, and some populations are readily recognised as vulnerable while others struggle for acknowledgment despite abundant evidence. We must resist answering selective outrage with selective outrage of our own. White South Africans deserve protection regardless of historical privilege. Palestinian suffering cannot be dismissed because Israel is a powerful ally. Nor should Nigerians demand acknowledgment of atrocities abroad while avoiding painful chapters of our own history. South Africa shows how political power can elevate an unsubstantiated allegation, Gaza how extensive scrutiny can still fail to move powerful governments, and Biafra how the struggle for recognition can outlive the violence. Genocide’s definition belongs to international law, its investigation requires evidence, and its prevention demands more than diplomatic convenience. Anyone may call something genocide. What matters is whose testimony is believed, whose evidence is examined and who can transform suffering into acknowledgment, accountability and action. Until those judgments transcend race, religion, ethnicity, national convenience and geopolitical allegiance, the promise of never again will remain less a universal commitment than a selectively honoured one.
